speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPENSATION FOR CANADIAN LAND AND WATER RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the recent press statements by United States authorities that they are prepared to proceed with the Libby dam project, will the minister inform the house whether the United States proposals are sufficient to assure adequate compensation for the use in perpetuity of Canadian land and water resources?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO COMPENSATION FOR CANADIAN LAND AND WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of his question, which is of course of particular interest

Inquiries of the Ministry to the province of British Columbia. I should like to make a short statement in reply to it.
The hon. member is referring to an application which was submitted in January, 1951, on behalf of the United States government for the approval of the international joint commission of the construction of the Libby Dam project. This project would involve the construction of a dam on the Kootenay river at Libby, Montana, and the creation, upstream, of a reservoir flooding the Kootenay valley in Montana and for a distance of 42 miles in British Columbia.
Under the boundary waters treaty of 1909, a project such as this, which would affect the level of waters on both sides of the boundary, requires the approval of the international joint commission and of the governments of Canada and the United States. The government of British Columbia is also, of course, concerned in the matter since the project will involve the use and development of resources within the province. In a development of this sort consideration must be given not only to the question of compensation for property damages but also to the larger question of appropriate arrangements to ensure that those entitled to the benefits to be derived from the use of Canadian natural resources-in this case the people of British Columbia in particular and the people of Canada in general-should receive those benefits in full measure.
In putting the Canadian interest before the international joint commission, the Canadian government has therefore been concerned to ensure that benefits will accrue to Canada commensurate with the contribution which Canadian resources will make to the developed project. This is the matter that is at issue before the commission now, and I hope that it will be resolved soon. The development and use of natural resources within their boundaries is, of course, a matter within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. The Canadian government is making every effort to see that the needs and rights of the people in the area concerned are fully met and that the government of British Columbia is given every opportunity to present its views to the international joint commission so that the interests of the people of British Columbia can be fully protected.
I understand that, following recent discussions with the Canadian chairman of the international joint commission, the government of British Columbia, continuing studies initiated by the previous government of the province, is seeking the advice of a committee representative of public and private interests

as to the policy to be recommended to the international joint commission with regard to compensation and to the distribution of the benefits of the project to those entitled to them. I can assure my hon. friend that the Canadian government, whose approval is also required before any project such as this can be undertaken, will ensure that the interests of the people of British Columbia will be given full consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. Waison MacNaughl (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: PROTECTION OF COASTAL FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. speaker, the main purpose of this bill is ;o protect Canadian fisheries in territorial md inland waters from encroachment from Eoreign fishing vessels and to regulate the ;onduct of foreign fishing vessels in our ;erritorial and inland waters.
This bill is a revision of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 43, which was first enacted in 1868 in an act intituled "The Foreign Fishing Vessels Act". This act was amended several times over the years, the last of which amendments was made in 1913.
The present bill is largely one of clarification and revision. A few obsolete provisions of the present act are removed.
Under the present act the governor in council may issue permits to United States dshing vessels to enter Atlantic ports to purchase bait, ice, seines, lines and all other supplies and outfits and for the transshipment of catches and the shipping of crews. The governor in council, however, has no power under the present act to grant similar privileges to fishing vessels of any other foreign power.
Previous to the entry of Newfoundland into the union certain privileges and arrangements had grown up whereby fishing vessels of foreign powers, particularly of Portugal, were permitted to enter Newfoundland ports. At the time of union the governor in council was given authority by section 9 of the Statute Law Amendment (Newfoundland) Act, being chapter 6 of the statutes of 1949, to issue permits to fishing vessels of foreign powers to enter Newfoundland ports. The governor in council has no power to issue permits to the fishing vessels of any foreign power to enter Canadian ports on the Pacific coast.
The present bill will give the governor in council power to issue permits to the fishing vessels of any foreign power to enter any port in Canada. This power, however, will in no way affect the reciprocal port privileges on the Pacific coast for fishing vessels of the halibut fleet, which are regulated by treaty between Canada and the United States.
The present act purports to exclude from our territorial waters foreign fishing vessels. There is, however, no definition in the act of what constitutes a fishing vessel. It is doubtful whether, in its ordinary sense, the term "fishing vessel" could be construed to include vessels hunting seals or taking marine plants in our territorial waters. There is also serious doubt whether the present act

would exclude vessels that are not engaged directly in fishing, that is fish processing vessels or even mother ships, which do not engage in actual fishing but which store or transport fish caught by catching boats. It was therefore thought desirable to include in this bill a proper and complete definition of the term "fishing vessel."
The present act provides for forfeiture only as a penalty for foreign fishing vessels entering our territorial waters. In days gone by this was probably all right, but today, having regard to the value of trawlers, it is far too drastic a penalty. This bill therefore provides fines as alternative methods of punishment. By way of revision this bill provides a simplified procedure for seizure and forfeiture of any foreign fishing vessels. The procedure in the present act was deemed to be too cumbersome, involving great delays and expense.
Under the present act enforcement was vested not only in Canadian but also in British naval vessels and officers. The present bill provides that enforcement shall be the responsibility only of Canadian vessels and officers. The present act was designated as the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act. Since the act is no longer used for purposes of customs administration but entirely for fisheries protection against encroachment of our territorial waters by foreign fishing vessels, it was deemed desirable to change the name of the act accordingly.
The present act only excludes fishing vessels which are "foreign or not navigated according to the laws of Great Britain or of Canada" and which are not permitted to come in by "any treaty or convention or any law of Great Britain or of Canada". This bill would bring the law into conformity with the present status of Canada within the commonwealth and all fishing vessels, except Canadian fishing vessels, would be prohibited from coming into our territorial or inland waters unless permitted by a treaty or law of Canada.
The present bill has come to us from the Senate where it received very thorough consideration. It is intended that when this bill has had its second reading it will be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries.

They could catch bait and export it to these foreign fishing vessels when they were a few miles off the coast, and the purpose of the government was to try to prevent any trade of that kind with foreign fishing vessels so that they would not be put in practically the same position as the fishermen of Newfoundland.
Why were they doing that? Traditionally these countries had been using the Grand Banks for centuries, but because of the development of a national spirit on this side of the water we in Newfoundland felt-and I suppose the fishermen of the maritime provinces felt the same way about it-that, since we were so close to this natural resource, this great supply of fish, we had greater rights, or if we did not have greater rights there was no reason why we should go out of our way to help fishermen who had come across from Europe so that they could be in the same position as Newfoundland fishermen.
Portugal, Spain and Italy were great importers of Newfoundland codfish, and certainly up until the beginning of the first world war took tremendous quantities of Newfoundland fish. They were our principal export markets. During the first and second world wars it was not very easy to export salt fish to those countries, but since Portugal and Spain were neutral countries, large quantities of salt codfish could still be sent to them. However, since the second world war and because of the development of the bad exchange position, neither Spain nor Portugal has been in as good a position as formerly to purchase our fish. Spain particularly, on account of having undergone a civil war, was in no position to buy and has bought very little fish for many years. Portugal, however, did.
During the past fifteen or twenty years all countries have been paying more attention to the prosecution of the fisheries, and Italy, France, England, Spain and Portugal have embarked on a deliberate policy of increasing their fishing fleets. So far as Portugal is concerned, it still has a large fleet of what we call bankers in Newfoundland. These are vessels which use dories. One man goes out in a boat and catches fish by the use of the trawl that I described a little while ago. The other countries particularly, and Canada as well, now use vessels which are called trawlers. The trawls are not like the small hand trawl but are machine-operated trawls, and the vessels using them are better known to the trade as draggers. By trawling or dragging a big net across the smooth bottom

of the banks they take in huge quantities of all kinds of fish that are there, big and small.
Until a few years ago the policy of Canada was to prevent vessels of that kind being operated off the Atlantic coast, but the government of this country could not prevent the Spaniards, the British, the French, the Portuguese and the Italians using their draggers, and they have been using them and catching great quantities of fish. Canada also uses draggers. In 1951 the fishermen of Newfoundland, as I mentioned the other day, formed a federation. I believe it was the secretary of the organization who a short while ago criticized the policy of the government in permitting foreign fishing vessels, especially those of the Portuguese, to come to Newfoundland and get supplies not only of bait but of other things that they need to carry on the fisheries, and then catching large quantities of codfish to take home and because of this purchasing less Newfoundland salt codfish.
It saems to be a foolish policy for the government to permit foreign fishing vessels to come here and be fitted out and assisted in every way in catching codfish to be cured in Portugal while at the same time the Portuguese market for salt codfish has been declining. I understand that the position taken by the Portuguese is that at the present time they cannot get the kind of fish they want. They say they want larger fish than the Newfoundland trade is able to supply. Most of the large fish are used in supplying fresh and frozen fillets for export to the United States. Therefore there is only a small quantity available for sale to the salt codfish markets.
Recently the Portuguese did purchase a mixed quantity of 35 per cent large and 65 per cent small fish, but only under pressure. I have heard no statement from the parliamentary assistant with respect to what the attitude of the government is going to be on this matter. All we have is a bare statement similar to what was given in the other place which gives no more information than can be ascertained by looking at the bill that is before us with the explanatory notes on the side. It seems to me there is not sufficient information contained in the bare statement of the parliamentary assistant for the house to get a proper understanding of this legislation. I know that this is going to be applicable to all of Canada, but how far, practically, will it be effective in other parts of Canada, apart from Newfoundland? Foreign fishing vessels coming from Europe seldom use ports other than Newfoundland. I understand some of them went into Sydney up until July 1 when that was stopped. I do not know how

the practice originated and it would be interesting if either the minister or his assistant would tell us how they came to do that if it was illegal. What is going to be the policy of the government in regard to a matter of such vital importance to Newfoundland? The minister or the parliamentary assistant might also tell us what is going to be the position in so far as Newfoundland is concerned especially. I know this concerns the Pacific coast but I would like to know how it affects us in Newfoundland at the present time.
We would like to know what countries have the right by treaty to go into Newfoundland waters at the present time? I understand that United States vessels have that right although they do not exercise it. Have any other countries got that right? Are the other laws to which I referred as being in effect in Newfoundland, the Foreign Fishing Vessels Act of Newfoundland and the Export and Sale of Bait Fishes Act, going to be continued in force? I understand that, under the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada the laws in effect regarding fisheries are to continue for five years, except ithat by agreement with the provincial government they may be altered. Has there been any agreement or is there any intention of altering those laws regarding those fishing vessels entering Newfoundland, or the export of bait fish?
I said a few moments ago that we had a wonderful supply of bait fishes. They have some of these bait fishes in other parts of Canada as well. First of all there is herring, a fish that is quite common and which can be found along the maritime coast as well as that of Newfoundland. Then we have caplin. I am not sure but my hon. friend from Gloucester could perhaps tell me whether they have caplin in New Brunswick. Caplin are small fish, something like smelts. They come in millions all along the coast of Newfoundland and are very useful bait for certain periods. Then, of course, we have the squid, which is the most valuable bait of all. I think it is found chiefly in Newfoundland waters.
Recent developments in connection with the abandonment of fishing vessels pure and simple-that is, using hooks and line-is something upon which we should have a pronouncement some time or other. I understand that, following the Maclean report back in 1929, Canada is against the use of draggers. At the present time there is an attempt being made to have an international agreement upon the question to what extent they can be used. There is no doubt about it, they are

There is another type of fishing going on out there which the Spaniards are using. It seems to me, if we prohibit foreign fishing vessels from going into our ports that by the use of mother ships such as the parliamentary assistant has referred to or by the use of St. Pierre and Miquelon as a base for supplies, they could get around the difficulty of supplies even if they could not get bait. speechtext:
I do not
intend to prolong the debate on this bill, Mr. Speaker, because I understand that it is going to be considered by the standing committee on fisheries. There are, however, one or two points that I should like to bring to the attention of the house at this time. This bill deals with the protection of the fisheries, and its scope is therefore restricted to our territorial waters. In my province some of the best fishing grounds, which would be called inshore fishing grounds, lie outside territorial waters about 15 or 20 miles off shore. I realize that the very best way to obtain protection of those fisheries is by an international agreement with the countries concerned. For that reason, I am following with a great deal of interest the progress that is being made in this direction by the northwest Atlantic fisheries commission. We know from experience, however, that international agreements take a long time to negotiate. In the meantime, I

feel that some thought should be given to the extension of our territorial waters.
Some years ago Norway submitted a case to The Hague court, which tribunal I believe handed down a ruling which endorsed the principle of headland to headland in delineating the territorial waters of that country. I doubt if even that ruling would afford very much protection to the fishing grounds in my province. In any event, I believe it is worth giving some thought to, and I should like to see that principle applied by drawing a line from Cape Sable to Cape Race. This would ensure the protection of the major part of the fisheries in the Atlantic provinces. If that does not prove feasible, I think the time will come when we shall have to give some thought as to whether or not we might extend our territorial waters to the continental shelf.
Now, when the former minister of fisheries was introducing his estimates last year, I believe it was June 19, the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) mentioned that foreign ships were permitted to have free entry into Newfoundland ports, while at the same time they were excluded from the ports of Halifax and Sydney as well as other ports in the maritime provinces. In reply to that question, the minister pointed out that this was due to an old ruling which had been allowed to lapse during the years of war, and was being more strictly enforced. He promised that the situation would be taken care of when the bill was revised, as is being done in the measure we have before us.
When he was replying to the member for Cape Breton South, if I remember correctly, the Minister of Fisheries expressed the hope that these permits which foreign countries would have to get would be used as a sort of bargaining power between the countries concerned and ourselves. When the member for Cape Breton South raised his question, I think he had in mind the fact that certain firms in the maritime ports were placed at a disadvantage in comparison with Newfoundland firms at St. John's. I believe we all agree that all firms in all parts of Canada should have equal rights and no firm should have one advantage which does not apply to the others. The relationship that existed in Newfoundland was not only an advantage to the merchants of St. John's; its main feature was the bargaining power which it gave us with Portugal, to whom we sold the major part of our salt fish.
I believe the time has come when we must again begin to use some of our bargaining power with Portugal. The friendly attitude which we felt that Portugal always had for

us seems to be deteriorating in these later years. We find that they are now driving a much harder bargain than they used to do. They insist upon having the choicest fish, and insist upon fish from Newfoundland of a higher standard than they are prepared to accept from other countries. Last March I had to bring before this house a situation in which some Portuguese draggers were dragging in territorial waters and becoming a menace to inshore fishermen from my riding. Also, we have reason to think that some of these Portuguese trawlers offer such high prices to the Newfoundland fishermen for bait that they are no longer interested in getting bait for sale to our cold storage plants, which are the only source of supply for our Newfoundland fishermen. The only other point I should like to make, Mr. Speaker, is that any comparison between the advantages enjoyed by merchants or business firms in the maritime ports with those enjoyed by the merchants in Newfoundland ports tends to set up a sort of conflict of interest between the two provinces. I suppose in a competitive system such a thing is normal, and so long as it remains on that level between firms in one province and firms in another province I do not think we should worry too much about it. But the thing that worries me now is that we have removed that situation from the local level of individual firms and placed it on a provincial level, and now it becomes a conflict of interest not between firms but between one province and another.
If a situation should ever arise in which Newfoundland, in order to export its fish, or in order to ensure European markets for fish, should wish to have those permits rescinded, I can see that the people in the maritimes would raise some opposition to it. That would be a situation which would tend to mar the unity of purpose and the unity of interests which should exist between one province and another in this great nation of Canada.
I have just one more point, Mr. Speaker, and that is this. While we are considering the protection of the fisheries I should like to point out that we need to protect our fishing grounds not only from foreign draggers but also from local draggers, because on those small inshore fishing grounds the local dragger can do just as much damage as a foreign dragger. These are very small areas, and once they have been dragged over for 68108-95

Mr. Speaker, this bill to protect the coastal fisheries does not affect any principle of any particular interest to the north shore of the province of New Brunswick, inasmuch as it is a rather rare occurrence that we have foreign vessels coming into our ports. I realize that at this stage of the legislation, according to parliamentary procedure, I am not supposed to refer to any particular section of the bill. I will do that when the bill reaches the committee stage. But I invite the hon. member for Prince and the legal officers of the Department of Fisheries to study this bill again and I am sure they will realize that there are prohibitions in this bill as against the master in command of a fishing vessel, and a fishing vessel according to legal interpretation, without any specification is general and could mean my vessel or my brother's vessel in Shippigan. It is in view of the fact that, according to its context,^ the proposed bill hits or could probably hit the Canadian fishermen that I rise on this occasion to bring this matter to the attention of the departmental authorities because, as the hon. member for Prince said in his remarks, higher fines and stiffer penalties are provided for infractions of this legislation by foreign vessels. I hold no brief for masters of foreign vessels, but I certainly would like the department to clothe with as much protection as possible our Canadian fishermen. In my submission,

Coastal Fisheries
there are dangers and apparent dangers, from the wording of this bill as it now reads, for the masters of our own Canadian vessels.
There are certain sections of the bill which make the entry of even a Canadian vessel into our own territorial waters an offence, and the same penalties in such a case would apply against the master of a Canadian ship just as they would apply to the master of a foreign ship. I submit, sir, that that is unfair.
I said a moment ago that the fines were considerably increased, and so they are. In some instances the fines provided by the former act are increased over fifty times what they were, and in other instances twenty-five times what they were heretofore. Again I say, as regards the masters of the foreign vessels I am not concerned, but I do say that such an increase in penalties for possible violations by the masters of our Canadian vessels is totally unfair.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is also an attempt .-I would not say it is intentional-in the terminology of this bill to take away from an accused, for instance, the master of a Canadian vessel who commits an infraction of this law, the possible defence that he would have of lack of intent. We have similar legislation in our Criminal Code, for instance, with respect to obstructing a peace officer. Hon. gentlemen know that this offence is triable in several alternate ways, first, by indictment; second, by summary trial, and third, by summary conviction. But the point I wish to make at this stage, Mr. Speaker, is that the offence provided by section 168 of the Criminal Code for obstructing a peace officer is prefaced by the important word "wilfully". Hon. members know that "wilfully" is synonymous with intentionally or deliberately.
The bon. member for Prince will admit that there is a similar infraction provided for in the bill now before the house, that of obstructing a protection officer. As I said before, when the bill reaches committee stage I shall refer more particularly to the section in question. The word "wilfully" is omitted from the offence of opposing or obstructing a protection officer, and I submit that this is most unfair, especially to any of our Canadian masters of ships, or seamen who might be taken to court on the offence of obstructing a protection officer under the proposed legislation.
Ever since I have been practising law, I have noticed that there is a general tendency in federal legislation to take away as much as possible from the individual certain rights and privileges which he has been guaranteed under both British and Canadian jurisprudence from time immemorial. Every new
[Mr. Roblchaud.l
piece of legislation that comes before this House of Commons, and those coming before some provincial legislatures, seem to try to take away, bit by bit, rights which we have enjoyed for centuries.

Hence I submit, for the attention of departmental officers, especially the legal officers in the Department of Fisheries, the points I have made, and suggest that they should reread the whole context of the bill. I am hopeful that they will agree with me in what I have said about the word wilfully, and I think they will also agree that possible offences are created by the bill which would apply not only to foreign captains but, in certain circumstances, unfortunately to the masters of Canadian ships. As I said before, realizing the limitations placed upon me at this stage in procedure, I do not believe I can discuss the matter further. I see my hon. friend, the hon. member for Prince, nodding his head, so that I should think he is already seized of the point I have made at this stage. Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to go over the ground already covered by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), or by my colleague the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter).
This bill will have far-reaching effects on the fishing industry in the province of Newfoundland. As I see it, the bill itself is not as important as the authority it will give in the matter of making regulations. The regulations will be the deciding factor in the reception accorded the bill by the authorities in Newfoundland.
In that province we shall have a serious situation if the regulations are enforced so as to debar foreign vessels from coming to our ports for supplies. It will affect adversely the pleasant relations we have had with foreign countries for hundreds of years. Anything that will upset the friendly relationship existing between Newfoundland and

Portugal for decades will be a serious thing for Newfoundland. We sell and have sold large quantities of salt fish to Portugal. Although we want to be in a position to bargain with them, we do not want to be in the position of dictating to them.
If the regulations to be made as a result of the passage of this legislation are used in a dictatorial manner, they will be detrimental to the relations which have always existed between Portugal and Newfoundland. And what applies to Portugal applies also to Spain and possibly to Italy.
At the present time a situation is developing on the Grand Banks off the coast of Newfoundland pointing to depletion. As some hon. members will know, the Grand Banks have been the breeding ground for countless millions of fish for decades. It is the feed brought up by the gulf stream and deposited on these banks which feeds the fish and nurtures them. From that breeding ground countless millions of fish come to the shores of Newfoundland year after year.
There is now evidence that depletion is taking place in certain areas of the Grand Banks, and if this continues it will certainly affect shore fishing in Newfoundland. We need some protection there. The only way I can see to bring this about is by international agreement with those countries which use large draggers and up-to-date modern trawlers which are coming in increasing numbers to Newfoundland waters, and fishing in our waters, or off the coast of Newfoundland, year after year.
Anyone who will go to St. John's in the summer can see them by the dozen, running up to a tonnage of about 2,000 tons. They can catch, cure and store huge tonnages of fish-and they have been doing it. We do need protection, so far as the Grand Banks are concerned, or depletion will take place in that area as it has taken place off the coast of Nova Scotia, and the coast of New England in the United States.
If our regulations are made so as to give us bargaining power whereby we can make agreements with those foreign countries which fish in our waters, then I am all for them. But if we use those regulations as a means to dictate to other countries what they shall do, then I say we are in danger of upsetting the friendly relationships we have had with those countries for many years.
It is the policy of Portugal to be selfsupporting in its supply of fish. Because of intensive fishing by the Portuguese they do not need such great quantities of fish from Newfoundland. We may have a point in the 68108-95i
Coastal Fisheries
regulations whereby we can induce them to increase their purchases from us by giving them certain concessions in connection with getting supplies, and fishing in Newfoundland waters.
As I see it, the bill is all right; but what will come from the bill, and what regulations will be used to make our position as a fish-producing and exporting country better than it has been, is what is really important.
Then, making reference to territorial waters, or the three-mile limit, it is possible tbat some hon. members may not know this demarcation was brought about by the international court at The Hague many years ago because of action taken by the then government of Newfoundland. I find upon reading the bill that it gives power to designate what shall be coastal waters. What do you mean by that? Are you going to make it twelve miles or twenty miles? This bill and the regulations which will follow will have far-reaching effects on the fisheries of Canada, particularly those of the province of Newfoundland. I do hope that when it is before the committee it will be given the closest scrutiny so that we will have legislation which will be worthy, not only of the province of Newfoundland but of the whole of Canada. I think it is time that we had such legislation, but it must be scrutinized from all angles so that no province in this great country will be penalized by what we do here.
I listened with considerable attention to the parliamentary assistant and I realize that there are many points that need to be clarified. If he can clarify them to my satisfaction I shall be very happy. The people in Newfoundland are viewing this bill with some concern and they are taking it quite seriously. are to be interpreted as being within three miles from land, foreign vessels would still be permitted to enter many of our bays and waters which we look upon as being territorial waters. spoke to me about this bill and indicated that they thought it was good legislation. Mr. Speaker, those who have taken part in the debate this afternoon have all represented constituencies on the Atlantic seaboard. This bill, though possibly designed largely to meet conditions on the Atlantic coast, will also apply to the Pacific coast. Therefore I feel it is only right that I should say a few words with respect to the application of the bill to the Pacific coast, particularly as it will be a long time before we will have an opportunity to discuss it in committee of the whole inasmuch as I understand it is to be referred to a special committee. No great help will be given to the fisheries industry of the Pacific coast unless Canada defines quite clearly her territorial responsibility over the waters adjacent to the coast.
At the present time there is no clear-cut definition even of the so-called three-mile limit. Up to a few years ago the line from which the three-mile limit extended was taken by general international agreement to be from the low-water mark which follows the various indentations of the coast line. I think it was in December a year ago that the Norwegian government appealed to the international court respecting the definition of their territorial waters and particularly how
Coastal Fisheries
the base line should be drawn along their coast. As a result of the Norwegian claim a number of points were selected along the coast line. Sometimes these were on the coast, sometimes on islands, and sometimes even on rocks at a considerable distance from the mainland of Norway. These points were then connected by straight lines running from point to point and by the use of these straight lines the waters claimed to be territorial waters of Norway were designated.
On the Pacific coast the strait of Juan de Fuca separates the southern portion of Vancouver island from the state of Washington. Under an international agreement a straight line was drawn down the centre of that strait. When you clear cape Flattery, a point in the northwest section of the' state of Washington, the description of the territorial waters then ceases. But a practically straight line can be drawn from a few miles to the west of Victoria, certainly from the entrance of the strait of Juan de Fuca, which would run in a northwesterly direction clearing the headlands of the west coast of Vancouver island, clearing Queen Charlotte islands and joining with the international boundary line in Dixon strait.
The advantage of a clear definition of territorial waters by a very nearly straight line is that it would be possible for protective craft to recognize if there were foreign vessels poaching in those waters. Fisheries protective craft would be able to see that the regulations imposed by Canada were being carried out in these clearly defined waters. Unless it is possible to define our territorial waters clearly, it will not be possible to establish full jurisdiction over them, and until we can establish jurisdiction over these waters, which are frequently inhabited by fish that we harvest at various times, it will be impossible to provide adequate protection for our fishing industry.
There are two great areas of inland water which are excluded from being considered as territorial waters if the three-mile limit following the indentations of the mainland coast of British Columbia is accepted. These are of course Queen Charlotte sound and Hecate strait. A very high percentage of the fish harvested on the Pacific coast frequent these two bodies of water at one time or another. I consider that it is imperative that these waters should be included and designated as Canadian territorial waters. We must have jurisdiction over them if we ever hope to provide adequate protection for the fishing industry of British Columbia. At least 50 per cent of the salmon caught for canning purposes are caught beyond the so-called three-mile limit. Fish which are beyond territorial waters are fair game for the fishing

Coastal Fisheries
vessels of any country. Therefore I feel that the first thing which must be done is to define our territorial waters, the waters over which we can and will exercise jurisdiction. Otherwise we cannot begin to offer protection to our fishing industry.
There is one other point I would like to refer to in this bill. There must be adequate means for enforcing the regulations which are made. This bill indicates steps which will be taken when vessels are seized for infractions of the rules and it is noticeable that there are different regulations for seizure and forfeiture of foreign vessels on the Atlantic coast than exist on the Pacific coast. I suggest that what is sauce for the goose is also sauce for the gander. If vessels from European countries are being seized for infractions of the regulations on the Atlantic seaboard, and are being tried by Canadian courts, then surely the same sort of provision should exist for foreign vessels infringing on the regulations covering Canadian territorial waters on the Pacific coast. If those vessels are seized, their captains and masters should also be tried in Canadian courts instead of being handed over to a foreign country for trial. I feel that the provisions which exist on the Atlantic coast should be applicable on the Pacific coast.
I will finish by once more emphasizing the fact that unless our territorial waters on the Pacific coast are clearly defined no real protection can be given to our fishing industry. Clear definition of those territorial waters must be made from a more or less straight base line. The best and in fact the only line which can be acceptable to the fishing industry of British Columbia is a line which includes as territorial waters those great fishing grounds of Queen Charlotte sound and Hecate strait. It is a simple process to draw a straight line on the western shores of Vancouver island to Queen Charlotte island. I am not sure whether it is necessary to go as far into the ocean as the edge of the continental shelf but it is essential that a clearly defined line be drawn on the west coast of those islands.
Such a line could not interfere with any international shipping because international shipping coming from Asia would be clear of those territorial waters until it entered the strait of Juan de Fuca. Ocean liners crossing the Pacific are still considerably west of the continental shelf as it runs north from the strait of Juan de Fuca paralleling Vancouver island on the west coast.
I hope that most careful consideration will be given to this bill when it goes before the
[Mr. Pearkes.l
standing committee to ensure that full protection is given to the fishermen of British Columbia by defining these territorial waters and by making them include grounds which our fish frequent and where so much effort, time and money has been spent in conserving different species. I also hope that consideration will be given to having the same means of enforcing the regulations applicable on both east and west coasts of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to say very much on this particular bill but I do agree with those who say there is a muddle so far as our territorial waters jurisdiction is concerned. They were wise enough, intelligent enough and observant enough to get the name of one of the American vessels that was there. They made their complaint, as I think they should have done, to the officers in Halifax, and I have no doubt that those officers took the matter up here. Nothing was done about it. I wrote to the department the other day, and I must say that as far as the officials are concerned, in Ottawa and perhaps everywhere, the department is splendidly managed. In my letter I pointed out that these were poor people, that they had small boats-small trawls-and I got an answer to the letter to the effect that the fishing protective boat went out and looked at the situation. It appeared as if the American trawler which had destroyed their nets was within the three-mile limit but the government boat was not sufficiently equipped to indicate, by cross bearings, exactly where the trawlers were. The department said they had another case at Yarmouth, and I think it was the case brought by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk). They said that they had asked the Department of External Affairs to warn the United States vessels to keep off our shores.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is good enough. I think there should be some way of reimbursing these people. They have the name of that vessel and there

should be some way of reimbursing these poor fishermen without their having to go to the necessity of bringing an action. As a matter of fact, they are not able to do that because of their financial situation.
I have been looking over this bill and I do not know exactly what the department proposes in matters of this kind. Section 6, of course, says:
Whenever a protection officer suspects on reasonable grounds that an offence against this act has been committed, he may seize
(a) any fishing vessel-
And so forth. That is all very well when the protective vessel finds the offending vessel within the three-mile limit; but what is going to happen when the vessel goes in there, does damage to these poor fishermen, and then leaves the jurisdiction of Canada? I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am not finding fault at all with the departmental officers in Ottawa or anywhere else, but I do believe they should at least take a little more interest in such matters as I have brought before this house. This bill, Mr. Speaker, is described in the explanatory note as one to replace the present Customs and Fisheries Protection Act. For the first time we have the word "coastal" appearing in the title of the bill. It is to be known as the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. It is described as an act to protect the coastal fisheries. Now, those words "coastal fisheries" are not defined in the act, but there is a reference to Canadian territorial waters. I suggest to Your Honour that the foundation for the whole bill is the
Coastal Fisheries
definition of Canadian territorial waters. If the definition is not clear, then there is great uncertainty about the whole bill.
It does seem to me that the most important question to be considered by the standing committee on marine and fisheries is this question of what are Canadian territorial waters. It is quite appropriate that that should be decided by the marine and fisheries committee, because "territorial waters" involves our fisheries more than any other activity in the country. I cannot quote from the bill itself, but if hon. members will refer to the interpretation section they will find that there is nothing definite there about this question of Canadian territorial waters. I believe that the only conclusion anyone could reach, if the bill remains as drawn, is that the three-mile limit is to be the test. I do not believe that is satisfactory in the year 1953.
During consideration last year of the draft international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean, this same committee considered the problem of Canadian territorial waters. The question gave the committee some difficulty, and I notice that in the report tabled on June 10, 1952, there was a reference to that question in these words:
Your committee was also aware of the great importance of further extending improved international co-operation and good will so that in the near future such matters as the territorial waters' limits, after thorough study and investigation, may be resolved.
I urge that the committee go into this question thoroughly in its sittings during the present session.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) has outlined very clearly our wishes concerning the territorial waters of the Pacific coast. We believe that the line should be drawn in such a manner that the water between Vancouver island and the Queen Charlotte islands, which is known as Queen Charlotte sound, and the strait between the Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland of British Columbia which is called Hecate strait, should be declared by Canada to be Canadian territorial waters.
I do not believe we are likely to make much progress in meeting this question of what are and what are not territorial waters unless this committee on marine and fisheries takes the lead. I hope that will be the course followed in the committee during this session.

speechtext:
Hon. members will recall
that the federal government has extended financial assistance in the past to various projects of a major character which were designed to conserve the water resources of an area and which also were of benefit in reducing the hazard of serious floods. Among these was the Shand dam in the Grand river watershed in Ontario, where federal government participation through the Department of Public Works from 1939 to 1942 was part of the over-all program designed in part to assist provincial governments in relieving unemployment. In 1950-51 assistance was also extended in the case of the Luther marsh dam, through the Department of Public Works. This dam, also in the Grand river watershed, was regarded as a necessary adjunct to the Shand dam.
In 1951-52, through the engineering and water resources branch of the Department of Resources and Development, the federal government participated in the cost of constructing the Fanshawe dam on the Thames river north of London, and through this department we have also informed the government of Ontario that the federal government will similarly participate in the proposed Glen Allan dam on the Conestoga river. These projects were all considered on their merits. They were regarded as special cases to which federal assistance, on behalf of all the taxpayers of Canada, could reasonably be given because of their nature and magnitude.

The bill referred to in this resolution seeks authority to provide a legislative basis for federal assistance for water conservation projects of a major character across Canada. The projects which would receive assistance under the bill would be, in general, of a similar type to those I have already mentioned, and federal government participation would be considered only upon an appropriate request from the provincial government concerned.
It should be emphasized that the conservation of natural resources within ithe provinces is primarily a provincial responsibility, and that this proposed bill does not in any way seek to establish any change in jurisdiction or responsibility. The federal government would have no proprietary interest in works towards which it might contribute.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is one which should have been introduced in the house many years ago. As a very young boy in the province of Ontario I remember witnessing the death of a neighbour at a level crossing. He was a very fine old gentleman with a large family. He was proceeding to town with his team and there was a light snowstorm. The train bore down upon him and he met his death. I suppose since that date twenty others have died at the same crossing. One of the advantages of coming a long distance to attend the House of Commons is that as one travels across Canada one sees very many phases of the life of the country, and the level crossing menace is one which is growing more horrible as the days go by.
At the town of Deroche in British Columbia there is a level crossing, and thirty years ago a whole family of six was killed there. That
Railway Act
was the Macdonald family who were descendants of John Sanidfield Macdonald, a great man in Canada at the time of confederation and before. The mother and her family of six were wiped out at that crossing, and every year since fatal accidents have been occurring at the level crossing at Deroche. It is all right to give a great deal of attention to the raising of freight rates and the salaries of the employees of the railways. These are very necessary things, and as important matters they must be dealt with. But it is equally important that we should give more attention to the protection of the lives of the people of Canada so far as level crossings are concerned. I believe there is a field there where the leaders of the labour unions should take a very active part in arousing public opinion.
I have a letter here from a mother whose little girl was killed at a level crossing in Ontario at a point near Woodstock. If I were to read it to the house it would bring tears to the eyes of all present, especially those who have children of their own. It is a crossing which is not properly protected. I have noticed that boards of trade and other public-spirited groups across the country have erected crosses at level crossings to mark where fatal accidents have occurred.
I was in the county of Perth the other day and while there had occasion to notice a particular crossing near the residence of the member for that beautiful constituency. We got over it safely, but it is a very dangerous crossing. It is elevated high above the level of the surrounding countryside. I am enough of an engineer to believe that the cost of putting a subway under the track would be less than it cost to provide the earth fill necessary to raise the pavement up to the level of the track.
I have made some inquiries as to the number of fatal accidents in Canada last year, and I find that in the first ten months of 1952 the total number of people injured at level crossings was 453. Of this number 166 were killed and the total number of accidents was 357. Some of those involved died and some were crippled for life. That was the harvest in the first ten months of 1952. at level crossings throughout Canada.
I am eager to assist the construction of better transportation facilities in every way, and I know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) works day and night towards the same end. In British Columbia we managed after some years to persuade the government of the province, assisted by the government of Canada, to extend the Pacific Great Eastern Railway into the northern part of the province. In November of last year

Railway Act
eighty miles of construction were completed and a celebration was held at the city of Prince George to mark the institution of rail service from the south over the P.G.E.
I know that hon. members have heard me refer many times to that railway and the need of extending it farther north, even to Alaska. I think we are all pretty well agreed now that it should be done, and even the Social Credit government of British Columbia has pledged itself to extend the railway. I personally have championed the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern for thirty years or more, and now we have an extension of eighty miles from Quesnel to the crossing of the Fraser river at Prince George. Before they started construction I said: Surely we can avoid level crossings on this splendid new rail line we are opening up in the northern part of British Columbia. Well, they thought they could and then they thought they could not.
I travelled over the line recently, and I believe there are twelve level crossings in the eighty miles. In other words, twelve opportunities are provided to reduce the number of citizens of the Cariboo by fatal accidents at level crossings.
I notice from the estimates that the government spends $1 million a year to eliminate or reduce the hazard of certain level crossings. I know it would be a very big undertaking to remove all level crossings in Canada because there are many thousands of them, but I suggest to the house it would be a very easy matter to pass the bill and start afresh on the problem. We could help to solve the problem by not allowing any more level crossings to be built where new construction is involved. It is just as simple as that.
I doubt if it would add very substantially to the cost of building railways if engineers were instructed to avoid level crossings, and we would establish the principle that to build another death trap, another level crossing, would be a violation of the statute law of this country. We are building highways in the north and west and all over this country. This bill, I hope, will also make unlawful the construction of a new highway over a railway and certainly the construction of a new railway over a highway.
You may say that the age of railways is fast coming to a close, but I think that is far from the truth. We will be building hundreds of miles of railway in Canada long after hon. gentlemen who are listening to me now are out of this house and probably called to their reward; because the very nature of our country will call for the construction of railways.

I would say that the riding which I represent in this house is larger than that part of Ontario which lies south of a line through Sudbury and Port Arthur. Our population, of course, is scattered and there is room in that great area of Canada, in the adjoining riding of Skeena and in the Yukon, for a very large population. I visualize a day when the largest percentage of the people in British Columbia will live north of Prince George. The land is certainly there, with broad valleys and all the natural resources- mineral resources, oil, natural gas and so on. This matter of the construction of railways is very important and of considerable public interest today in my community.
There is a project designed to extend the Northern Alberta Railways westward from Hines Creek into British Columbia and on toward the area I referred to. It is not something that will be done in the dim and distant future. It is something that should be done as quickly as we can do it, because the area is already settled. In one area people are hauling their goods one hundred miles or so to the railway, even one hundred and twenty miles, trying to make a success of farming. They are hauling their goods farther than it is from here to Montreal. I need not say that construction of that bit of road would be sound business. It should be done at once, and when it is done it will be one of the most profitable sections of the Northern Alberta system.
How ridiculous it would be, Mr. Speaker, to proceed with the building of that railway and to build level crossings there so that farmers going to market would be compelled to face the hazard of death and disaster at those level crossings.
As I understand it, the first railway in western Ontario was built 101 years ago. Sir Francis Hincks, a famous man in Upper Canada in those days, was the promoter of that railway. I would like to have a list of the casualties that have occurred at level crossings between Sarnia and Hamilton or between Sarnia and Niagara Falls. The figure would be atrocious. Of course railways are always built on the best and most level property; they are built where the population is dense and by the very nature of things where traffic is greatest.
We have made so much headway in so many lines of endeavour, yet in the simple matter of protecting our people from the hazards of level crossings we remain practically as we were at the time of Sir Francis Hincks. At some crossings there is very little or no protection. At others there are rather expensive warning signals installed. I would

like to see the most modern devices established at each level crossing. The electric eye sort of thing might be brought into play. Down at Windsor station in Montreal the C.P.R. has installed electric beams so that when we go there with our grips our very passing opens the door. Similarly on existing level crossings modern electronics could very easily be employed to make them safer.
This bill which we have before us will ensure that on new construction the menace of level crossings will vanish for all time in Canada. I hope and pray that all hon. members of this house, irrespective of party, will get behind it, get it into committee, and assist in having it put upon the statute books of our country.

Certainly when one reads the statistics respecting railway crossing tragedies he cannot help but conclude that a responsibility rests upon us here to do whatever can be done in an effort to contribute toward the lowering of the number of these tragedies.
I am convinced that we can, through the removal of a great many of the level crossings, help to reduce the number of accidents that occur. It seems to me that a great deal of emphasis must be laid upon the importance of safety campaigns, and the assumption on the part of individual drivers of a greater share of responsibility than many of them up to this time have indicated they are prepared to accept.
After all, what constitutes a dangerous crossing? Frequently we refer to a crossing as being dangerous if the records show that a certain number of deaths have occurred through accidents at that crossing. But the evidence indicates that, conceivably in a majority of cases, those tragedies have occurred on level, open crossings where in many instances visibility extends a mile in either direction. I fully realize that the removal of as many level crossings as possible

Railway Act
will assist in solving the problem, but certainly we must also make efforts in other directions, perhaps through educational campaigns.
The bill refers to highways, but I think it is important to keep in mind that provincial governments in Canada have recognized the necessity of removing as many level crossings as possible when they have rebuilt or constructed highways. Everywhere in Canada there is evidence to indicate that the provinces are assuming responsibilities in that direction.
The hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) has mentioned the question of jurisdiction. It may prove to be an important point so far as the legality of a bill of this kind is concerned.

We think it is an absolute tragedy that people will continue to drive into the sides of trains, that in some instances they will pass a line of standing traffic and drive into an approaching train, and this has happened more than once. We know that on occasions they will drive up to a level crossing, stop, and then start across, only to be hit by an approaching train.
It occurs to me that a substantial contribution to a solution will be found in a greater acceptance of responsibility on the part of drivers, through educational and other campaigns that can be carried on. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ELIMINATE LEVEL CROSSINGS IN FUTURE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will be grateful to the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) for having introduced the principle of the bill, and for having brought once again to the attention of the house the very serious matters with which it deals. I believe the house is quite familiar with the question, because it has been discussed not only in debates on private bills but in debates on the estimates for the Department of Transport, as well as on other occasions.
One of the most serious problems with which we have to deal today is that of railway-highway grade crossings. It is a subject which has engaged the attention not only of people here in Canada but, before that, of experts and specialists in the United States, where the problem is far more serious than it is here.
I commend the hon. member for his desire to deal with this matter, but I must say to him with all respect that the amendment to the section of the Railway Act which he suggests does not begin to deal seriously with the problem. The government saw fit early

in the year, as was stated by the hon. member for Meadow Lake, to ask the board of transport commissioners to study the whole problem of railway grade crossings. It gave the board full power, as set out in order in council P.C. 1953/52, to make a complete and thorough investigation and study. I think it would be no compliment to the board of transport commissioners if at this stage the house were to say to it that it should do as set out in the bill.
Then there are several objections to the bill. The first I see is that it makes the implementation of this section mandatory upon the board. In other words the board would be obliged to force the railways to construct a grade separation after July 1, 1953, upon any application that was made. As it is today, the board has that power under the act. It is a discretion it has, and that discretion should not be taken away; because if it were taken away there would be no way of determining which crossing should have priority because of density of traffic or density of population or because of location.
With the section the way it is worded now I can see a situation where in an isolated part of Canada, at a place where there was little traffic, a railroad would be forced, perhaps in conjunction with the highway authorities, the municipalities and the like, to spend a large sum of money to separate a grade when there was little or no need for such separation in that particular area. I can think of a railroad building a spur line into an area which might cross a highway where there would be little or no traffic-this happens repeatedly-and the grade crossing fund or even the municipality and the railroad would be charged with the expenditure of a substantial sum of money when the grade separation was not really required.
Another objectionable feature is the mandatory provision. The board now has discretion, and it seems to me that it should continue to have discretion in these cases. I wish I had more time to depl with this matter because if I had I would make reference to a study that has been made of the railway-highway grade crossing problem by A. Kenneth Beggs of the Stanford research institute. This is an excellent document which goes into the problem very thoroughly. It gives the causes of accidents and in a series of excellent theses it proposes solutions to the problem.
The problem is a serious one. If we were to eliminate all grade crossings in Canada the sum of $100 million would barely suffice. If I had the time at my disposal I would
Railway Act
deal with some of the causes responsible for the increase of accidents, and I would deal in part with the solutions suggested.
I think the hon. member is to be complimented upon his attempt to find a solution. In his anxiety to eliminate these accidents he has submitted this amendment to the house. I know the amendment is well-intentioned, but it deals only with a small portion of the problem. In order to deal with the whole problem the government has asked the board of transport commissioners, which because of its statutory powers is able to consider problems of this kind, to make a thorough survey of the railway-highway grade crossing problem in Canada. When the board has made its report it will then be possible to bring down amendments to the Railway Act and perhaps the grade crossing fund. It will be possible to consult the provinces, because I think perhaps one of these sections impinges upon provincial jurisdiction.
I should like to say more on this subject, but it seems to me that I have said enough to indicate to the house that it would not be advisable to accept the bill in its present form. I would hope that the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray), having succeeded in raising interest in the subject and knowing that the matter is being studied by the board of transport commissioners, would see fit under all these circumstances to withdraw the bill.

All hon. members who have taken part in the discussions agree that the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole to consider a resolution preceding a money bill is debatable. the South Saskatchewan river irrigation project. The minister declared that this resolution, and I use his words, "does not embrace irrigation projects or irrigation policy."
I should like to quote further from Mr. Speaker's ruling of June 18, 1952. He said:
I should point out that the motion is for the Speaker to leave the chair, etc. It is not a motion to adopt the resolution. I am sure that is not the procedure contemplated by standing order No. 60, nor is it in accordance with Mr. Speaker Glen's ruling, in which I concur.

If any members are opposed to the resolution, and do not think that it should even be considered in the committee of the whole, or-
And I wish to underline these words.
-if they require additional information before agreeing to the motion, they should be given an opportunity to speak on the motion. The minister should endeavour to answer the objections which have been raised and to give the information requested.

Accordingly in my opinion the practice of the minister opening the debate on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to consider in committee of the whole a resolution preceding a money bill should be discontinued.
When the discussion on this subject was before the house the other night a number of members expressed concern over the difficulty which the Speaker would have in keeping the debate within the limits of the above interpretation. Mr. Speaker, I shall speak very briefly on the question of the conservation of water resources, with particular reference to the province of Saskatchewan, after which I shall move an amendment.
The situation in Saskatchewan, in so far as the conservation of water is concerned, is

very serious in various parts of the province. It is particularly so in the area referred to as the Palliser triangle. It is not something that is a novelty, because it has continued for generations. Only the other day I went back to the journal kept in 1856 by Captain Palliser, the great English explorer. He dealt with this subject in his diary on October 3, 1856, when the expedition was on the west bank of the South Saskatchewan river, at the Elbow.
He makes this entry in his journal concerning the valley running eastward of the South Saskatchewan river. He said his party were assured that in flood times this valley connected with the Qu'Appelle valley. He was very much interested in the idea of water conservation and communication between the South Saskatchewan and the Red river settlement, and used these words:
The valley containing the Red Deer lakes resembles in width that of a large river; it is said to cross the South Saskatchewan 12 miles below the Elbow and is said to run continuously and to join the valley of the Qu'Appelle by the Last Mountain lake. I was assured by the half breeds that there was hardly any obstruction beyond one low portage existing to cut off communication by this route in the spring with those lakes which are west of the Qu'Appelle river; information which is highly suggestive of a more minute engineering investigation as to the expense and feasibility of a connection-
And so on. He goes on to point out that as the years go by the need for water conservation in Saskatchewan, or in that part of Saskatchewan, will correspondingly increase. Then a little later on, in 1859, a report was made to the legislative assembly of Upper Canada pointing out that the area now known as Saskatchewan, and part of Alberta, needed something to be done in order to conserve moisture, for periodically that area found itself arid and unproductive.
Very considerable has been done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. That act, it is well to remember, was introduced by the Bennett government, and was sponsored by the Hon. Robert Weir, the then minister of agriculture, in order to do something to improve the situation in those parts of the prairie provinces where, as a result of drought, production ceased.

Agriculturally-minded Saskatchewan has never regained peace of mind since the terrible drought of the 30's which laid it in the dust.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution we have before us precedes a measure for the conservation of water resources under the terms outlined in the resolution, and provides for a payment by the federal government of 37J per cent of the cost of the various projects that may come under this legislation.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, although it may be technically correct, as the minister says, that this resolution deals only with water conservation, nevertheless it cannot help but have a bearing upon the soil resources in various parts of Canada. If you are conserving water resources for the prevention of floods, surely one of the important reasons for the prevention of floods is to prevent damage to agricultural lands. That being the case I say that this resolution and this legislation is in the wrong department; not because I have not the greatest respect for the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) but because I feel that any proposition dealing with water conservation must at the same time affect the conservation of our soil resources, and should be in the Department of Agriculture.
I am very disappointed indeed with the niggardly contribution that the federal government proposes to make toward any project developed under this particular legislation. Reviewing other projects in the past, the government here took the position that it should pay the total cost of large capital

works and that any subsidiary costs should be paid by the provincial authority. The provincial authority may derive some of the necessary funds from citizens who receive definite advantage from the project. In any large project that has been finalized the federal government's contribution, instead of being something over one-third of the cost, has been approximately two-thirds of the over-all cost of the project.
Other projects, and especially one other major project for Saskatchewan, if dealt with by this resolution would be most inadequately covered because the proportion of the sums involved which the federal government is prepared to advance is in my opinion very low, far too' low, and would not be a satisfactory basis for the general conservation of water resources. I protest, Mr. Speaker, along with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), the fact that in this resolution, and in the statement which the minister gave to the house this afternoon, there is no provision for water conservation on the South Saskatchewan river in the province of Saskatchewan.
It has already been pointed out how important water is to that province. The hon. member for Lake Centre mentioned a number of municipalities and the cost to the government through P.F.A.A. and other payments. I might mention 36 municipalities in the central area of Saskatchewan which over the years have cost the public treasury some $29 million in relief payments and over $15 million in prairie farm assistance. That is a total cost to the federal treasury of well over $40 million.
That area of Canada, the central portion of Saskatchewan, needs water conservation in the worst way. Certainly I feel that it is not only in the public interest in the sense that we should help our Canadian citizens living in that part of Saskatchewan, but it is also in the public interest from a financial standpoint; because unless there is adequate water conservation and utilization in that area there will be a further burden of many millions of dollars on the federal treasury in the years to come.
I hope that, while we have been unable to discuss a development that is in the minds of many members this evening on this motion that is before us now, the minister who is piloting this resolution through the house will discuss the matter with his colleagues in the cabinet and make certain we are given a chance at an early date to debate the other matter which we all have in our minds, that is the South Saskatchewan river project, so the people of Saskatchewan may also have a

chance of obtaining a program and a project that would provide them with real water conservation in that area.
Mr. Speaker, this resolution comes from the wrong department. The resolution makes a mockery of water conservation when it does not deal with the project that is in the minds of most members. I say to the government that in order to discharge their responsibility, particularly their responsibility to the people of western Canada, they should provide a water conservation measure under which payments far above the 37J per cent set forth here can be made. I would say, as a matter of fact, that any percentage less than two-thirds of the total final cost of the project is something less than the government should provide.
I am disappointed, as I have said, that this project is not in the Department of Agriculture. The agricultural institute of Canada, in a submission to the government earlier this year, made reference to this very legislation which was forecast in the speech from the throne. They contended that any conservation of water resources that affected the soil in any way, shape or form, should be dealt with by the Department of Agriculture. On page 1 of their brief, they had this to say:
We have learned th^t the government of Canada proposes to present to the present session of parliament legislation concerning the conservation of water resources.
That is the legislation we are discussing now.
It is the opinion of the institute that unless such development is entirely exclusive of actual water conservation relating to agriculture, it would lead only to serious duplication of effort, wastage of public funds and considerable confusion.
I say this resolution proves that there is duplication in the matter of water conservation. If we are to get efficient management of our water and soil resources; if we are to get adequate conservation, then the authority handling the conservation of water resources should also handle the conservation of soil resources, and that authority should be in the Department of Agriculture.
We are extremely disappointed that this resolution has not made provision for that project which is dear to the hearts of the people of Saskatchewan, no matter to what political party they may belong. We naturally hope that a member of the government will bring forward a proposition at an early date that will provide for that project. Moreover, whether or not the government decides to carry out the requests that I have made, I trust that the government will delay no longer in giving parliament an opportunity
