The question of water conservation is one which affects the entire continent of North America. It is not merely a question of the construction of a few dams. It is not merely a question of localized grants to provinces and it is not, as I hope to ishow, purely an agricultural problem. The' problem of water conservation enters the whole economic life of the country. I want to mention the case of the three prairie provinces. It is hoped that the three prairie provinces will gradually become industrialized, as have the states on the great plains in the republic of the United States of America. The economy of these states has become more co-ordinated and has not been subjected to the difficulties of a one-crop economy, with all the devastating fluctuations which take place in a country or a province with that type of economy.
The question of water and industrialization is perhaps one of which hon. members do not realize the importance. The consumption of water industrially is simply stupendous, and and I propose to give a few figures to show what the industrialization of a country means in terms of water consumption. For instance,

Water Resources
the production of a ton of rolled steel requires the consumption of 110,000 gallons of water. This water is completely dissipated in the form of steam and in other ways. The production of a ton of rayon yam takes 250,000 to 400,000 gallons of water; a barrel of aviation gasoline takes from 1,050 gallons of water, if made from the natural product, to as much as 15,000 gallons of water if made synthetically.
If we are ever going to help the west industrialize, the problem of the water table ground water supply is just as essential as the other minerals which will be necessary to make the west an industrial area. Therefore when we talk about the conservation of water, particularly in the west, we are not merely dealing with the taboo subject, which of course I shall not mention; we are dealing with the very basis of the economy of the whole country.
The precipitation in North America south of the northern limit of cereals is approximately 30 inches a year, and for Canada this works out to about 5 billion acre-feet of water. An acre-foot is the term used for discussing water supplies on the land, meaning a depth of one foot of water over an area of an acre. This tremendous amount of water is only partially used by man. Most of it is either wasted or is disposed of in what is known as the run-off. Irrigation, domestic, municipal and industrial use is probably less than 100 million acre-feet in Canada out of about 5 billion. The United States figure is 160 million acre-feet.
We have in North America two-thirds of the world's supply of surface water. That is a conservative estimate. The surface water is lakes, streams, and water which is, as the name implies, on the surface, but differs of course from ground water which is under the surface. The ground water supply which we have at the moment is equal to about thirty years of annual precipitation. In other words the ground water at any time is equal to about thirty years of run-off; but despite this abundant source of ground water we have in the last few years suffered a shocking drought because we have been negligent in the conservation of our water supply. We have permitted excessive run-off; we have depleted in certain sections the ground water; we have lowered the water table until some places in the province of Saskatchewan are unsuited now for industries because of the lack of ground water.
That is something we cannot let go without endeavouring to correct it. Where you have a condition of the soil brought about by carelessness, by bad management, by lack of conservation which has destroyed the ability

of that area to have a balanced economy, then it is time something more than those steps which are envisaged in this resolution is done. It is for that reason that I think this resolution is inadequate.
We go on from the question of ground water to the question of evaporation. The term which is used is evapo-transpiration, and it accounts for about two-thirds of the total precipitation every year. As the climate over the last fifty years has definitely shown that it is slowly but steadily warming, the transpiration is increasing and the evaporation due to the warmer climate is much greater than it was a quarter or a half century ago; and as the trend is continuing the question of conservation becomes, with every fraction of a degree increase in temperature, a very much more serious problem.
I shall not go into the details of water use and discuss the matter in any technical terms, but let me say this. Our North American cities use approximately between 150 gallons and 160 gallons per capita per day; whereas the European cities use fewer than 40 gallons of water per capita per day. It is on that use of water that a very great deal of our income and our high standard of living is based. If we allow our surface water to run off in the excesses to which it is doing in many rivers today, or if we allow the water table to sink lower and lower and become depleted, we will endanger the metropolitan life of our country.
If you want to realize how serious that can be you have only to look back to 1949 and 1950 at the terrific catastrophe that was narrowly averted in the city of New York when the reservoirs of that city practically dried up. Despite our apparent abundance of water, the same thing could happen here. I live on a small creek that used to be a salmon river. It has not had a fish in it for 25 years. Yet in the middle of the last century it was a salmon river.
The trend is still going on. We do not see it, because we do not measure the destruction of our water supply with a scientific instrument. We say, "What a pity it is that the old swimming hole is not what it used to be." Or we say, "What a pity it is that the old creek is not full of water, and has no fish in it any more."
The reason it is not as it was before lies in the fact that we are scandalously wasteful of the greatest heritage we have, and that is our water supply. We are more profligate in the waste of water than in perhaps anything else. I speak tonight on this resolution because I feel this whole question of the conservation of water is one which must be

taken as a permanent, long-term problem, not merely as a resolution brought in concerning a few check-dams.
It has to form a part of the basic thinking of this country because, Mr. Speaker, despite the abundance we have, despite our amazing riches we can, as we have in parts of Canada, destroy this great heritage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me we have been so long away from the subject matter of the resolution it might be fitting to place on record just what it states. The resolution we are discussing is as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize grants of assistance to provinces for the conservation of water resources under the terms and conditions specified in the said measure, such grants not to exceed thirty-seven and one-half per cent of the-
And I understand the words "cost of the" are to be put in there.
*-projects; and to be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the above mentioned purposes; and to provide that all officers, clerks and employees required for carrying out the provisions of the measure shall be appointed in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
I should not like to go very far away from the excellent speech just delivered by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) before commending him. I believe he has made a real contribution to the information of hon. members and the country, and I think his warning voice is lifted not one minute too soon.
I do not hesitate to say that I am heartily in support of this resolution. Our group has felt that this was not a resolution under which we should be discussing any irrigation project at all. This resolution, as it says, is purely for the conservation of water. That is why we have supported Mr. Speaker's rulings in both cases; and our names will appear as having voted contrary to members of the C.C.F. and the Progressive Conservative party. It is not that we are not deeply in sympathy with the development of water reservoirs and irrigation systems but, according to our understanding, that kind of thing will be taken care of under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which at the present time, as everyone recognizes, is an excellent measure and is being administered with what I consider to be great wisdom, courage and progressiveness.
I do not think it is fitting that members in opposition should be everlastingly finding fault with the government when the government is doing a good job. When it is doing well I believe in telling it so, just as I believe that when a man is living a good life one
Water Resources
ought to tell him a little bit about it before he dies, and should not be content with sending him flowers after he dies. I am not hoping that the Liberal government will die, but I will say that, in my judgment, since it took office in 1935 this government has administered the P.F.R.A. with what I consider to be laudable wisdom and progressiveness.
Before going further may I express sympathy with the British Columbia members who have sought to have the operations of P.F.R.A. extended to their province. I see no reason why that should not be done; in fact I see a good many reasons why it should be done.
Then turning to the resolution, may I say again I believe it is a laudable one. I am not saying that it goes far enough. I do not say that the hon. member for York West was extreme in pointing out what he considered to be deficiencies in the resolution. However, I look upon it as a very good one, because it is a step in the right direction. It is a first step, and a good substantial one, when the government undertakes to pay 37J per cent of the cost of water conservation projects undertaken jointly by the provinces and the dominion. Perhaps we shall see a better provision before long; but, as a start, I think this is a very good one, and I desire to voice commendation for it.
I should like to revert to the general subject the hon. member for York West has discussed. In addition to offering my congratulations, I should like to give him support. For the benefit of those who live in parts of Canada remote from areas most affected by this resolution, I would point out that we have in the three prairie provinces an enormous area known as the Palliser triangle, to which the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has already referred this evening. I, too, made reference to it in my remarks a year ago in support of the South Saskatchewan dam.
This Palliser triangle is a potential source of very great wealth, if it is properly managed.	It can be a source of great
calamity to this nation if it is not wisely managed. Somehow or another we must make provision for wise management of the Palliser triangle. True, we have great crops, sometimes year after year, in that area. But there is hardly a year in which there are not numbers of farmers in that region who lose their crops because of drought. There have been years when that whole country has been threatened with dust-bowl conditions.
Those times can come again. What should we be prepared to do to implement this resolution? In the first place, as has been

Water Resources
pointed out several times during the session, we have a watershed on the eastern slope of ithe Reeky mountains. Much has been done already by the provinces and the federal government through wise co-operation by way of making provision for the adequate protection of the forests on the watershed. I know, however, that the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) realizes that much more must be done.
There are great stretches on those mountain slopes where the forests have been denuded. Each of those slopes from which forests have been removed is a threat to the water supply of the Palliser triangle. We have to look forward to a time when we shall reforest our mountain slopes that have been denuded by settlers and by fires. That would cost a lot of money but it is one of the things that must be looked after, perhaps under the provisions contemplated by this resolution. Far too little water is falling in Alberta and Saskatchewan to meet the needs of the Palliser triangle in respect of irrigation alone. In addition to irrigation we have the needs of the cities-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after your experiences tonight I do not wonder that you are meticulous in the application of the rules. But I was not going to discuss irrigation; I was simply referring to the need of water for irrigation. In addition to those needs there must be water for the settlements. That need is increasing. Cities like Regina, Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Lethbridge, Medicine Hat and others across these plains will require more and more water, and provision must be made for them to have more water. That provision must be made before we go too far. I am not sure that enough care has been taken to look forward to the increasing needs of our cities and settlers as far as water for domestic and industrial uses is concerned. I take it that one of the objects of this resolution is to have all such matters looked into and to take the necessary measures while still there is time.
A good deal of the area in the Palliser triangle at least will have to be regrassed. This will have to be done on a large scale. Wind erosion has been very notable in many parts, and water erosion has been great. As a means of protecting the soil against erosive

elements we shall have either to regrass or cover with some other vegetation. This will cost money. I would imagine that such measures will be covered by this resolution.
In addition we need more forest fire control. There are nowhere near adequate means for protection against fire, although much progress has been made in the last fifteen years. We are still terrified when a forest fire breaks out because we are never sure it will be brought under control. We should spend enough money to enable us to check an ordinary forest fire in a reasonably short time. The devastation wrought in British Columbia and Alberta by forest fires during my memory is something we cannot afford to allow to continue. Otherwise we shall just not have the means of conserving water or providing ourselves with the wood we need.
Then there is the matter of dams and reservoirs, not for irrigation but for conservation. There are many places in the mountains where, by the building of dams, we could reservoir a great deal of water. There are many lakes which could be filled. I am sure the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelc'h) will be mentioning one of these, Sullivan lake, in connection with the Red Deer diversion area which is so dear to his heart. There are many lakes like that throughout the country which could be filled with water which now runs to waste in the spring or in times of wet weather during the summer. A great deal of this water could be conserved by the strategic building of dams.
I have mentioned only two or three matters in a rambling sort of way. I did not expect to participate in this debate. I have meant what I have said as in the nature of support for the resolution. As I remarked at the beginning, I commend the minister for introducing the resolution. It is a progressive resolution; I propose to support it. I intend to back any additional provisions such as this as long as I am permitted to remain in this house.
On motion of Mr. Herridge the debate was adjourned.
